stem: According to recent whole-mouse-brain cell atlases, where does the greatest diversity of discrete neuronal cell types reside?
choices: Isocortex, hippocampus and the striatum
Brain stem, hypothalamus/thalamus and pallidum
Cerebellar cortex and the deep cerebellar nuclei
Olfactory cortex and the cortical subplate
answer: Brain stem, hypothalamus/thalamus and pallidum
label: Atlases · where type diversity lives

stem: In the whole-brain atlases, how did subregions of the brain stem and hypothalamus differ in cell-type make-up from subregions of the cortex and striatum?
choices: Their subnuclei repeated shared types; cortical and striatal subregions had discrete, bespoke types
Both repeated the same shared types, differing mainly in total neuron count
Their subnuclei had discrete, bespoke cell types; cortical and striatal subregions repeated shared types
Both had discrete, bespoke cell types, differing mainly in their connectivity
answer: Their subnuclei had discrete, bespoke cell types; cortical and striatal subregions repeated shared types
label: Atlases · duplication vs bespoke

stem: Which structures do the authors group into the 'learning subsystem', sharing an architecture of repeated simple units?
choices: Cortex, thalamus, pallidum and hippocampus
Hypothalamus, striatum, cerebellum and amygdala
Cortex, brain stem, cerebellum and thalamus
Cortex, striatum, cerebellum and hippocampus
answer: Cortex, striatum, cerebellum and hippocampus
label: Learning subsystem · membership

stem: Why, in the authors' account, can cortical areas doing visual processing, math or language share highly similar cytoarchitecture?
choices: Their content is set by inputs and training data, not by their cell types
Their functions differ through area-specific transcriptomic cell types
Their functions differ through distinct neuromodulator receptors
Their content is set by hypothalamic cell types projecting to each area
answer: Their content is set by inputs and training data, not by their cell types
label: Learning subsystem · general-purpose hardware

stem: What scaling law do the authors propose relates neuron count to number of cell types in the learning subsystem?
choices: Superlinear power law: types rise rapidly with neuron count
Sublinear power law: neurons grow vastly, types stay nearly constant
Linear scaling: types grow in proportion to neurons
Exponential scaling: types double with each doubling of neurons
answer: Sublinear power law: neurons grow vastly, types stay nearly constant
label: Learning subsystem · scaling law

stem: In the authors' machine-learning analogy, what does the learning subsystem's neuron count correspond to?
choices: The reward function
The training data set
The number of model weights
The learning-rate hyperparameter
answer: The number of model weights
label: Learning subsystem · ML analogy

stem: What expansion of the hominin cortex relative to chimpanzees do the authors cite as enabled by decoupling size from cell-type complexity?
choices: It tripled in size over about 2 million years
It doubled in size over about 20 million years
It grew by half over about 6 million years
It doubled in size over about 6 million years
answer: It doubled in size over about 6 million years
label: Learning subsystem · hominin cortex

stem: What did molecular analyses reveal about von Economo neurons of the anterior cingulate and insular cortices?
choices: They are subtle variants of a conserved cell type
They are a primate-specific novel cell type
They are interneurons misclassified by morphology
They are steering-subsystem neurons that migrated into cortex
answer: They are subtle variants of a conserved cell type
label: Learning subsystem · von Economo neurons

stem: Beyond more copies of cell types, what do the authors say drives evolutionary advancement of the primate learning subsystem?
choices: Generation of novel transcriptomic cell types
Elaboration of synaptic connectivity
Expansion of neuropeptide repertoires
Recruitment of steering-subsystem cell types
answer: Elaboration of synaptic connectivity
label: Learning subsystem · connectomic elaboration

stem: Which software-engineering concept do the authors use as an analogy for the steering subsystem?
choices: A compression codec for world representations
A general-purpose operating-system kernel
Business logic for specific rules and edge cases
A load balancer replicating identical servers
answer: Business logic for specific rules and edge cases
label: Steering subsystem · business-logic analogy

stem: What example do the authors use to show that a seemingly simple reflex demands algorithmic complexity in the steering subsystem?
choices: The knee-jerk reflex, run by a spinal monosynaptic arc
Blinking, run by a cerebellar microcomplex
Pupil constriction, run by a cortical minicolumn
Swallowing, run by a medullary central pattern generator
answer: Swallowing, run by a medullary central pattern generator
label: Steering subsystem · swallowing CPG

stem: What architecture did work on the mouse gaze system reveal for coordinating head and eye movements?
choices: Single orienting neurons broadcast to separate modules per body part
One shared module computes head and eye commands together
Cortical minicolumns learn the coordination from experience
Cerebellar microcomplexes replicate one generic controller
answer: Single orienting neurons broadcast to separate modules per body part
label: Steering subsystem · gaze modules

stem: What scaling law do the authors propose relates neuron count to number of cell types in the steering subsystem?
choices: Sublinear power law: neurons grow vastly, types stay nearly constant
Superlinear power law: types rise rapidly with neuron count
Linear scaling: types grow in proportion to neurons
Logarithmic scaling: types saturate early
answer: Superlinear power law: types rise rapidly with neuron count
label: Steering subsystem · scaling law

stem: What do the authors say the limited cell redundancy in the steering subsystem supports?
choices: Greater capacity to store learned representations
Rapid gradient-based retuning of innate drives
Injury resilience, signal-to-noise and metabolic limits
Spare copies for later evolution into new types
answer: Injury resilience, signal-to-noise and metabolic limits
label: Steering subsystem · role of redundancy

stem: Why, according to the authors, does evolution keep favouring new cell types in the steering subsystem?
choices: They raise the storage capacity of learned world models
They lower the metabolic cost of existing circuits
They let cortical areas specialise for semantic content
They let organisms anticipate contingencies without trial-and-error
answer: They let organisms anticipate contingencies without trial-and-error
label: Steering subsystem · pressure for new types

stem: The adrenal cell type driving parental behaviour in the oldfield mouse is absent from the deer mouse; about how long ago did the two lineages diverge?
choices: About 20,000 years ago
About 2 million years ago
About 200,000 years ago
About 6 million years ago
answer: About 20,000 years ago
label: Steering subsystem · oldfield mouse

stem: In the authors' reinforcement-learning framing, what role does the steering subsystem play?
choices: The policy network
The reward function
The value-estimate critic
The replay buffer
answer: The reward function
label: Steering subsystem · reward function

stem: In human case studies, stimulating which steering-subsystem structures evoked complex emotions such as despair, shame and déjà vu?
choices: The prefrontal cortex and insula
The hippocampus and amygdala
The midbrain and hypothalamus
The cerebellum and pons
answer: The midbrain and hypothalamus
label: Steering subsystem · human stimulation

stem: How do the authors distinguish their steering/learning split from MacLean's triune brain or 'old brain vs new brain'?
choices: The split is phylogenetic; steering structures evolved first
The split is psychological; steering handles base drives
The split is developmental; steering matures before learning
The split is computational; both subsystems are ancient
answer: The split is computational; both subsystems are ancient
label: Frameworks · computational not phylogenetic

stem: Where do the authors place 'higher' motivations such as compassion, social bonding and curiosity?
choices: Innate drives encoded in the steering subsystem
Learned values stored in the learning subsystem
Emergent products of cortical-striatal loops
Cultural overlays with no cell-type basis
answer: Innate drives encoded in the steering subsystem
label: Frameworks · higher motivations

stem: How do the authors characterise plasticity in the steering subsystem, triggered by puberty, adiposity or dominance?
choices: Like gradient-descent updates of network weights
Like updating variables in business logic
Like adding new layers to a network
Like retraining a model from scratch
answer: Like updating variables in business logic
label: Frameworks · steering plasticity

stem: In the authors' caribou example of phenological mismatch, which cues do the caribou and their food plants each use for timing?
choices: Caribou use temperature; plants use day length
Both use day length, shifted by latitude
Caribou use day length; plants use temperature
Caribou use snow cover; plants use rainfall
answer: Caribou use day length; plants use temperature
label: Maladaptation · caribou mismatch

stem: Where have cell-type enrichment analyses of GWAS data placed genetic liability for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder?
choices: Midbrain dopaminergic and raphe serotonergic neurons
Hypothalamic arcuate neuropeptidergic neurons
Locus coeruleus and medullary noradrenergic neurons
Cortical pyramidal and striatal spiny neurons
answer: Cortical pyramidal and striatal spiny neurons
label: Disease · GWAS liability

stem: What do antipsychotics, antidepressants and mood stabilizers largely target, in the authors' framework?
choices: Neuromodulatory outputs of the steering subsystem
Cortical pyramidal neurons of the learning subsystem
Striatal medium spiny neurons of the learning subsystem
Cerebellar microcomplexes of the learning subsystem
answer: Neuromodulatory outputs of the steering subsystem
label: Disease · drug targets

stem: Why do the authors argue that pharmacologically dampening learning-subsystem components carries a heavy side-effect burden?
choices: Its rare cell types are too few to target reliably
Its shared hardware serves many functions, so cognition blunts broadly
Its neuropeptide receptors are expressed outside the brain
Its synapses regrow quickly, so effects wear off
answer: Its shared hardware serves many functions, so cognition blunts broadly
label: Disease · why not target learning

stem: What molecular feature of the steering subsystem's rare cell types makes it suited to targeted pharmacology?
choices: Shared ion channels across repeated modules
High expression of a single neurotransmitter transporter
Diverse neuropeptides and G protein-coupled receptors
A uniform AMPA receptor subunit composition
answer: Diverse neuropeptides and G protein-coupled receptors
label: Disease · neuropeptides and GPCRs

stem: In modulating addiction behaviour, where does GLP-1 act according to the authors?
choices: One cell type in the ventral striatum
Pyramidal neurons of the prefrontal cortex
A handful of cell types in the hippocampus
Hundreds of cell types in brainstem, hypothalamus, pallidum
answer: Hundreds of cell types in brainstem, hypothalamus, pallidum
label: Disease · GLP-1 targets

stem: In the authors' account of GLP-1 agonists treating addiction, what sequence ends the addictive behaviour?
choices: Steering devalues the drug, then learning extinguishes the behaviour
Learning devalues the drug, then steering extinguishes the behaviour
Steering blocks drug memories, then learning stops retrieval
Learning weights are frozen, then steering resets the drive
answer: Steering devalues the drug, then learning extinguishes the behaviour
label: Disease · devalue then extinguish

stem: In Alzheimer's disease, roughly what loss of CA1 pyramidal neurons makes hippocampal dysfunction reliably detectable?
choices: About 5%–10%
About 20%–30%
About 50%–60%
About 80%–90%
answer: About 20%–30%
label: Neurodegeneration · CA1 threshold

stem: Why do the authors argue stereology misses neuronal loss in most steering-subsystem populations?
choices: Steering neurons regenerate faster than they can be counted
Steering neurons are too densely packed to segment
Losing a few hundred rare cells is within counting noise
Steering populations are lost uniformly, leaving no contrast
answer: Losing a few hundred rare cells is within counting noise
label: Neurodegeneration · rare-type noise floor

stem: What do the two best-characterised vulnerable steering populations, substantia nigra dopaminergic and locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons, have in common?
choices: Both are the rarest types in the brain stem
Both express GLP-1 receptors
Both are enriched for schizophrenia GWAS signal
Both are visibly pigmented
answer: Both are visibly pigmented
label: Neurodegeneration · pigmented populations

stem: About what fraction of substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons is lost when Parkinson's motor symptoms emerge, as cited by the authors?
choices: About 30%
About 10%
About 50%
About 80%
answer: About 30%
label: Neurodegeneration · Parkinson's threshold

stem: What caveat do the authors give about the absolute number of steering cell types across species?
choices: It rises steadily from rodents to primates
It may not track phylogenetic advancement
It is fixed across all mammals
It tracks total brain neuron count
answer: It may not track phylogenetic advancement
label: Conclusion · no phylogenetic ladder

stem: What constraint do the authors suggest may cap how many discrete cell types a genome can generate?
choices: The number of protein-coding genes in the genome
The metabolic cost of each additional neuron
How many epigenetic states a genome can stably hold
The skull volume available for subcortical nuclei
answer: How many epigenetic states a genome can stably hold
label: Conclusion · upper bound on types

stem: What temporal asymmetry between the two subsystems do the authors use to reframe 'diseases of modernity'?
choices: Steering updates in a lifetime; learning needs evolved cell types
Both update within one lifetime, at different rates
Both need newly evolved cell types, over similar timescales
Learning updates in a lifetime; steering needs evolved cell types
answer: Learning updates in a lifetime; steering needs evolved cell types
label: Conclusion · temporal asymmetry

stem: What trade-off of RLHF do the authors cite as consistent with alignment being imposed post hoc?
choices: Lower benchmark scores, higher rated usefulness
Higher benchmark scores, lower rated usefulness
Higher benchmark scores and rated usefulness
Lower benchmark scores and rated safety
answer: Lower benchmark scores, higher rated usefulness
label: AI · RLHF trade-off

stem: How do the authors recast the AI alignment problem in light of the steering subsystem?
choices: Data scarcity: too few human preference labels
Architectural under-specification: no built-in steering
Over-parameterisation: too many model weights
Compute limits: training runs that are too short
answer: Architectural under-specification: no built-in steering
label: AI · architectural under-specification

stem: What research strategy do the authors say the steering subsystem's diversification scaling demands?
choices: Finding shared canonical micro-circuit principles
Modelling one representative nucleus in depth
Exhaustively characterising thousands of cell types
Scaling up recordings of cortical minicolumns
answer: Exhaustively characterising thousands of cell types
label: Conclusion · research strategy
